Glass =

A pane across the middle of a wall cell. You and the monsters see through it, bolts and shots stop on it, four hits crack then shatter it. The level kit lets windows into the walls between rooms and carves sealed observation rooms off corridors: control rooms, offices, labs, cells, nests, a vault. Inside are chairs, consoles, the station's dead, and sometimes something alive. Shoot the glass and it can get out.

Try it

  • Sector 1, the window at map 1 ; tp 45.5 19.5 180. Kick it with F or shoot it.

Matrix stations @ !

A data station sits in a wall near a sealed door. Press Space at it and you jack in: every wall, floor and ceiling becomes a neon wireframe grid, the lights go flat and bright, and the real world's monsters and things fade out. You have 50 seconds to grab the data cores scattered round the station while ICE sentinels hunt you. Get them all and the station opens its sealed doors. Run out and you're thrown out, 10 damage, try again. It has its own synthwave track and NEXUS lines.

Try it

  • Sector 1: the station is at tp 13.5 10.5 180, then Space.
  • Console: jackin, cores, jackout win.

Level editor F2

Your doc's design, built as described: the first-person edit mode is the game itself, frozen, plus a ray from the crosshair. The map from above paints the map's characters with the mouse and has layers for lights and heights. Tab drops you inside to build where you aim. Every change rebuilds the level live and keeps you where you stand. Ctrl+S writes the level file and keeps the old one as .bak.

To make that possible the levels moved out of DATA lines into neon-caster/levels/level1.txt and on: plain text, the map one character a cell, sections for zones, lights, events, heights, lifts and triggers. The level kit (levels.py) writes and checks the same files.

Keys

  • Map view: click to paint, right-click to pick up, Shift+drag for a box, wheel or [ ] to change glyph, L lights (1–8 colours), H heights, T to put you there, PgUp/PgDn sector, M monsters, U HUD.
  • Walking: click builds onto what you aim at, right-click knocks it down, E picks it up, T F V cycle the wall, floor and ceiling pictures live, Z repaints the floor, L/K add or remove a light, PgUp/PgDn raise or lower the floor (Shift: the ceiling).
  • Everywhere: Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+S save, F2 back to playing.

Heights, pits and lifts

The audit you asked for: the OpenGL renderer was already true 3D, so heights there meant building floors and ceilings at each cell's height plus step faces between cells. The software raycaster had about a third of it: the rising shutter already drew "a partial slice over what's behind it". What it lacked was continuing past a change in height and clipping, so it got a Doom-style column renderer. Each column walks front to back, closing in from below and above as ledges and lintels hide what's behind. It only runs on levels with heights, so chapter 15's Wolfenstein version still reads as before.

You step up anything to a quarter wall, fall off anything higher (and take damage if it's far), and need headroom. Pits kill. Lifts cycle on their own, work as elevators, or wait for a trigger. Sectors 1–9 now have a loot ledge with an elevator up to it, and 2–9 a raised dais under a high ceiling.

Try it

  • map 4: the dais is at tp 13.2 24.5 0; the ledge's elevator is at tp 13.5 6.5 180.
  • Console: raise X Y EIGHTHS, raise X0 Y0 X1 Y1 EIGHTHS ceil, lift X0 Y0 X1 Y1 LOW HIGH MODE SPEED.

Triggers and teleporters &

Triggers follow your trigger → action model, and the actions are console commands. So anything you can type, a level can do: open or lock doors, move lifts, slide walls away, put lights out, summon, teleport, play a sound, have NEXUS speak. A trigger fires when you enter a box (or cross a line), use a cell, clear the monsters out of an area, or after a time. Teleporter pads pair up in the order they're found on the map. Every sector got a teleporter shortcut and hint triggers.

Try it

  • trigger enter 20 20 22 22 : message AMBUSH | summon stalker 3, then walk there. In the console, | separates the actions; in a level file it's ;.
  • triggers lists a sector's triggers; trigger del N removes one.

QB64 code terminals $

Your "heart of it", in its first form. Press Space at a terminal: the doors near it slam and lock, NEXUS sneers "Repair my program? You will never open these doors", and a real QB64 program appears with its lines shuffled and words blanked. Put it back together and press F5: the game writes it out, compiles it with your qb64pe in the background (a COMPILING screen counts the seconds) and runs it. If it prints the right thing, the doors open. If it doesn't compile, you get qb64pe's own error. Wrong tries reveal hints, and after three the terminal fixes a line, so nobody gets trapped. Without qb64pe it checks the lines against the answer instead.

There are ten puzzles, easy to hard; sectors 1–9 each have a terminal, and the tenth puzzle waits for sector 10 to get one. Each teaches one idea tied to a course chapter: PRINT, variables, FOR/STEP, IF/ELSE, arrays, SQR and Pythagoras, SELECT CASE (monster states), FUNCTION, MID$/LEN, and AND 63 texture wrapping. I compiled and ran all ten for real before shipping them.

Keys

  • Up/Down choose a line, Shift+arrows move it, Enter fills its blank, F5 compile and run, H hint, Esc leave (the doors stay locked).
  • Any puzzle without the stakes: puzzle countdown. Write your own in neon-caster/puzzles/ (its README explains the format).

Monster and HUD editors

Both use one plain text format, as your doc suggested: [section] plus key = value, the same as the level files. monsters.txt holds every monster's numbers, and a new drops field: heavies drop shells 40% of the time, gunners cells, stalkers health, and the overseer always leaves a big medkit. The chapter 3 table in the code stays the default, so the course still reads the same. hud.txt holds where every HUD part goes, its bar size, colour, label and whether it shows, still in the 9px DOS font. The layout editor runs over the live game: drag parts with the mouse.

Keys

  • Monsters: PgUp/PgDn monster, Up/Down field, Left/Right change (Shift ×10), S save.
  • HUD: drag, Tab next, arrows nudge, V show/hide, C colour, +/- [/] bar size, S save, R reset, U done.

Art and sound while rtx is down

The overnight render queue never ran: rtx's ComfyUI fails every job in CLIPLoader, and soundmon waits forever on a failed job. So I drew the art in code (ENDESGA-32, 64×64) and synthesized the sounds with numpy. That covers the ten set pieces plus a chair and a fallen scientist, the gold thief and its wreck, ICE, data cores, the station and terminal walls, and the NEXUS portrait. On the sound side: kick, laser, plate, closet, power, hoard, glass, teleport, the thief's and ICE's sounds, and the network's music. All of them are stand-ins: pixelmon and soundmon can replace any file once rtx works again (it needs a restart on that machine).

Fixed along the way

  • Audio crash: about four starts in ten segfaulted in QB64PE's audio engine. The cause was a race between background sound decoding and the next _SNDOPEN. Loading "noasync" and streaming the music fixed it (0 in 24 starts after), and no longer keeps every track decoded in memory (well over 100 MB).
  • A one-second stutter whenever a monster closet opened. Creating a new GL buffer mid-game waits on the card. Rebuilt meshes now draw from normal memory until the next level.
  • Command line: arguments now also work when a launcher passes them as one string.
  • Editor rebuilds in GL: rebuilding a level could tell the GL side to rebuild halfway through. It now waits until the level is whole.
